title: The karma of relationships with parents and children

seo.title: Karma with parents and children in the destiny matrix
seo.description: Parents and children in the destiny matrix: what you took from the family line, what you pass on further, and how to break a repeating family script.
queries: arcanum of children in the destiny matrix
karma of relationships with parents and children destiny matrix
relationship with parents by date of birth

meaning: A family script usually gives itself away in a stray sentence: you hear your own voice and suddenly recognise the tone of a parent you argued with all your life. The section “Parents and children” exists for exactly these repeats — to notice what came from the family and what now gets passed on automatically.

In the product this view is built from three canonical points: the spiritual male line F, the spiritual female line G and the material male line H. They do not make up a separate formula for a child and they do not predict how many children you will have. The trio is a way of talking about family values and about everyday models of behaviour.

A strong reading does not hand out blame. It helps you split the inheritance: keep the ability to care, to hold your word or to stand up for the people close to you, without repeating the control, the silence and the strain that used to come with it. Then your parents’ way stops being the only script available.

Check the conclusions against real episodes: how people in the family asked for help, how they reacted to a mistake, how much freedom they gave and how they made peace after a quarrel. With no children of your own the section still works — read it through your parents and through the habits you pass on to younger people, to students or to friends, without inventing a forecast about offspring.

article_sections.h2: What the “Parents and children” section shows
paragraphs: The section gathers three canonical points: the spiritual male line F, the spiritual female line G and the material male line H. The first two are principles received from the family; the third is the way you carry them on yourself — how you explain, where you set a limit, what you praise, how you react when someone else gets it wrong. The trio describes family values and everyday models of behaviour, and the number of children stays outside it. What it does show well is the repeat: the sentence you swore never to say, which still flies out at the right moment. The section works for a person without children too — H appears in care, in teaching, in leading, in any relationship where someone more vulnerable stands next to you.

article_sections.h2: F — the rule of the male branch
paragraphs: Point F offers a guess about how the male branch handled responsibility, boundaries, movement and results. The arcanum names the principle; the facts come from you — sentences you overheard, decisions you know about, your own experience of talking to these people. The Chariot in this role, for example, keeps the rule “move fast and arrive first”, and along with that strength it passes on the heavy side: the habit of knocking people over at your own speed. When you know little about your relatives, it is more honest to leave the meaning as an open question and work on the rule you can see in yourself. Such a reading comes out shorter, but you can test it against a real episode.

article_sections.h2: G — the rule of the female branch
paragraphs: The female branch gives the second angle, and reducing it to care, feelings and housekeeping because of the name alone is the most common mistake. Here the arcanum names a way of acting that the household treated as the right one, and it is tested by the same facts: how people asked for help, how they reacted to a mistake, how they made peace after a row, how much freedom they gave. It helps to separate the skill from its usual price. The ability to support sits next to silence about your own needs; self-reliance sits next to difficulty in accepting help. Either conclusion is worth something only with an example: one case, one sentence, one episode you still remember.

The material male line shows what a person does with the inheritance next: how they explain the rules, where they set a limit, what they praise, how they hand out responsibility and what they say when someone else has got it wrong. The position becomes clear once you turn the noun into a verb: instead of “strictness”, say “I raise my voice every other time”. Then you can see what is worth keeping and which automatic reaction to swap for something calmer and more deliberate. The Lovers in this role, as in the reference chart, draw people in easily and demand a choice — and then pass on the habit of putting the decision off to the last minute.

article_sections.h2: F and G: two rules in one person
paragraphs: Start by comparing the two received principles with each other. They can pull together, or they can give different answers to the same situation: one branch says endure and keep your face, the other says walk out and slam the door. The point of the comparison is to catch the moment of the inner argument — which rule fires first, what it protects, whether there is a third move that keeps the value of both sides. Asking “who influenced me more” leads nowhere: both branches are already inside and argue in your voice. It is more useful to name the situation where you hear that argument most often; usually it comes back year after year.

article_sections.h2: From the rule you received to your own action
paragraphs: Match each branch against H separately: first F→H, then G→H. That shows what you carry on from the father’s rule and what from the mother’s, and keeps the two steps apart instead of blurring them into an impersonal “family total”. If the number in H matches F or G, the role is still different: a principle you received and your own action towards someone younger and weaker are not the same thing. One of the two steps is usually easy and already clear to you; the second shows up in small things — in your tone, in how fast you say no, in the way you explain your decision to a child or a student.

article_sections.h2: How to talk about family in the first person
paragraphs: Speaking in the first person changes the whole reading: “I learned”, “I keep doing”, “I want to change”. Even a family rule you have confirmed grew out of someone else’s circumstances — a move to another town, poverty, years when there was little to choose from — and it stops being a verdict on a relative. The section gives you material for your own choice; judging a parent’s character from a distance, or demanding that they accept your version of the past, takes the reading out of the area where it works. What you can change is your own way of speaking, of setting limits and of giving support — the part of the inheritance you can reach today.

Roles in the reference matrix 4–3–22 come out as 7–7–6. The Chariot stands in both the male and the female rule: both branches passed on the same thing — speed and push, arrive first. When both branches say one thing, the rule looks like the only possible one right up to the day someone says it out loud. The Lovers in the passing-on position change the question from “how do I make it in time” to “with whom exactly”. In practice it looks like this: a person is used to deciding fast, but what is asked of them is to choose, and the choice drags on to the last minute, because speed is no help in that kind of question. The repeat here matters more than the numbers themselves.

article_sections.h2: Practice: rewrite one rule you pass on
paragraphs: Pick a repeating sentence or reaction whose origin you know. Write down three lines: the use of the rule — what it gives; the price — what it costs; the H action — how it gets passed on through your tone, a ban, a condition. Then put together a new version so that the use stays and the other person gets the right to answer. Try the wording in one calm situation and judge the result by the quality of contact: did the conversation continue, did the person come back with a question. One rule at a time is enough — an inheritance gets rewritten line by line.

faq.q: What does karma with parents and children show in the destiny matrix?
faq.a: Three points: two principles received from the male and the female branch, and the way you carry them on yourself. The section collects family values and everyday models of behaviour, not the biographies of your relatives. What you get at the end is a list of what you want to keep and of what repeats automatically.

faq.q: Karma with parents in the destiny matrix — where do I start the reading?
faq.a: Start with facts: which sentence was repeated at home, how people asked for help, what they did after a row. Then put arcana F and G next to those facts and see which rule you recognise. A guess with no episode behind it is better left as a guess.

faq.q: What does the arcanum of children mean in the destiny matrix?
faq.a: There is no separate arcanum of children in the calculation: the material male line H covers the passing on. It describes your way of bringing someone up, explaining and setting limits, not the character or the number of children. It reads best as an action: what you do when a younger person gets something wrong.

faq.q: How do I read relationships with parents by date of birth?
faq.a: The date of birth gives two family arcana, F and G. Each is a guess about the rule of a branch, not a fact about a particular person. Check it against what you remember and know, and work first of all on the rule that is already running in your own behaviour.

faq.q: Does the section suit a person without children?
faq.a: Yes. H describes how rules are passed on in care, in teaching and in leading — anywhere your decisions affect someone more vulnerable. The method makes no forecast about a birth or about a child’s character.
